{"number":204,"title":"Pack environment requirements: corpus-owned generic script, packs declare the rest","body":"Closes #208.

Gives the corpus a **pack-driven cloud environment model**, so projects stop hand-rolling per-repo setup scripts and version hooks; the install logic lives with the technology.

## The model
- A pack declares what a web session needs in an optional **`env`** field (`label`, `setup`, `probe`). `setup`/`probe` may be a string **or a function of per-repo params** the project supplies in `.claudinite-checks.json` under **`packConfig`** (packs can require projects to state parameters about their usage — e.g. where `node` runs `npm ci`).
- **`packs/env.mjs`** drives it from the repo's *active* packs: **`install`** (run each fragment in the checkout), **`check`** (web-only SessionStart assert), **`plan`** (preview).
- **Pure probes, no version flag.** `check` asserts each requirement *directly* (Flutter on PATH, `node_modules` present) — the probes are the source of truth. A genuinely new requirement fails its probe and prompts a re-paste; the limited drift (a changed-but-still-present requirement) is accepted.
- **One corpus-owned generic script** — [`environment-setup.sh`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/pack-env-requirements/environment-setup.sh) at the corpus root, synced into every consumer's `.claudinite/`. Projects commit **no** copy; they wire the check hook and paste the corpus script (cd → sync → git hygiene → `env.mjs install`).

## First declarations
- **`flutter`** — the Flutter SDK. **`node`** — `npm ci`, per-repo `dirs`.
- The two git configs (`merge.ours.driver`, `rerere.enabled`) live in the generic script as cheap universal hygiene.

## Validation
- `node --test checks/test/*.test.mjs skills/*/*.test.mjs` → **104/104**; `node checks/run.mjs` clean; CI green.

## Consumers (separate PRs, depend on this landing + mount re-sync)
HelloWorldFlutterApp #14, GoogleCalendarEventCreator #668, ShoutsAndWhispers #7.

{"number":1464,"title":"Auto-merge policies: expected_outcome 'none'/'pr' plus a granular, built-ins-first automerge field","body":"Closes #1459

## What this is

The all-or-nothing outcome ceiling becomes a policy. `expected_outcome` collapses to `'none' | 'pr'`, and a `pr` task declares **`automerge`**: `'nothing'` (today's `open-pr`), `'anything'` (today's `merged-pr`), or a **list of diff classes** the policy engine measures the actual diff against. **Built-ins first**: every canon task composes the built-in classes with no configuration — improve-comments declares `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, growth-dedup `['markdown-line-removals']`, growth-extract `['doc-changes', 'file-additions']`, usage-fold `['generated-file-changes', 'single-file-code-changes']`, wiki-growth `['doc-changes']` — and no canon pack ships a `merge-rules.json`. The data extension stays for a task that genuinely knows a finer class than the built-ins can state. Negative terms veto (`reject:javascript-changes` works out of the box); anything unresolved fails closed; and no granular policy can cover a change to the policy sources themselves.

**A task.md describes the changes to perform, never what happens to them.** All landing mechanics — the delivery-settings nuances, the policy CLI, the item's `Merge:` field, the arming trailer — live only in `deliver-pr.md` (the agent lane's external procedure) and `land-pr.mjs` (the code lane); each worker doc is down to a one-line hand-off.

## The pieces

- **`packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`** — the engine: built-in classes (`doc-changes`, `readme-changes`, `comment-only-changes`, `test-changes`, `markdown-line-removals`, `file-additions`, `generated-file-changes`, `javascript-changes`, `single-file-code-changes`, `single-folder-code-changes`, and the `narrow-diff` composite `if-narrow` resolves to), the `merge-rules.json` compiler for pack-declared extensions, the verdict, and the CLI `deliver-pr.md` runs (`AUTOMERGE: yes|no`). Published via `shared-code/`.
- **Contract** — legacy `open-pr`/`merged-pr` normalize at the one door to the pair they always meant (advisory rename at author time, never red CI on an unedited member file); `verify-outcome` judges the pair, legacy spellings included.
- **`automerge-policy-scope`** (blocking, work scope) — self-gating on the `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy:` commit trailer a landing run stamps: quiet when nothing is armed, red when an armed diff exceeds its policy, so a mis-measured arm goes red before GitHub's queued auto-merge fires. usage-fold's code-lane delivery stamps the trailer too.

# revalidate-from-source worker

Reconcile the shelf's packs against the technologies they teach. A pack opts in by carrying an
`## Upstream` section in its `README.md`; this run reads what those sources have published since
each one's recorded anchor, and changes the pack's content where what it teaches has been dated.

**One PR against the default branch, for the whole run** — content changes and advanced anchors
together. Never merge it.

## 1. Take the opted-in set

Grep the corpus roots this repo curates for `^## Upstream$` in each `packs/<pack>/README.md`. That
set is the run's whole scope. A pack without the section is opted out: do not add one, do not
research it, do not mention it in the PR.

Each source is one line: what to watch, its URL, and `reconciled through <state>` — a date, a
version, a document revision. That trailing state is the window: you are asking what this source
has published **since** it.

## 2. Read each source

Fetch each source and collect what is new since its anchor. What counts as new is the source's own
unit: a published advisory, a release with breaking or security-relevant notes, a revised
specification or BCP, a deprecation announcement.

A source you **could not read** — the fetch was refused, the network policy blocks it, the URL is
gone — is *not checked*. Say so in the PR body, leave its anchor exactly as it stands, and
never infer what it would have said from search snippets or memory. A dead or moved URL is itself a
finding: propose the corrected one in the PR and leave the anchor behind it.

{"number":1060,"title":"Collapse chrome-extension-release into chrome-extension, and stop packs discussing each other","body":"Closes #1057. Four commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the reference sweep, and the cross-pack prose purge.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. Dropping either side would drop the member's own `config`, `rules` and `accept` — acceptances especially, since a dropped one brings its finding straight back.

**The `cer/` ids do not change**, for the same reason: `accept` entries name rules by id.

## A pack does not discuss its neighbours

Reviewing the collapse turned up the wider class: `firebase-release`'s README opened by saying it is declared "like chrome-extension". A `barriers` probe (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**, in two shapes:

- **Boundary/turf prose** — "sits under X", "that is Y's turf", a whole `## Boundary` section listing what the neighbours own. Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field — the field the pack directory routes a lesson by — so each site now states what the pack does *not* cover without naming who does.
- **Procedure pointers** — a rule delegating a how-to to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:` field, an executable command, and the comments on the dashboard's deliberate duplicates of sheepdog's helpers. Kept: the link is what makes the procedure findable, and restating it in both places is exactly what the corpus forbids.

22 references survive, all in the second class. No standing barrier rule was added — the probe was a measuring instrument, and it is not in the diff.

## Consumer safety

The shape the collapse newly exposes is an extension repo that codes but does not publish — the canon publishes no extension, so its own CI says nothing about it. `packs-tests/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` gains that shape (`codes-an-extension`), and a pack test asserts every release rule is inert on it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`, `engine/migrations/`** — the rename-map entry and the merge in `applyPackRenames`.
- **`engine/scheduler/signals/`** — the `release` signal carries whether the repo publishes, read off the checkout beside the manifest version it already read.
- **`packs/chrome-extension/`** — absorbs the release module, the seven declared checks (each gated), the stubs, the `store-release` task, both migration records, and `RELEASE.md` as the **`chrome-store-releases`** skill; manifest, README and RULES rewritten for one pack.
- **`packs/firebase`, `firebase-release`, `google-identity`, `jwt`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`, `executable-requirements`, `spec-driven-product`, `web-scraping`, `git-github`, `sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `basics`** — neighbour prose removed, and in the release packs' case references to the pack that no longer exists.
- **`.github/`** — the core workflows README, and the retired pre-vendoring release copies' own naming.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on every pack whose content changed; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

The two migration records keep their wording — they describe arrangements true when they were written.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2200 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).
- The merge and both drift-guard directions seen red before the code that fixes them; the crossing count re-measured after the purge.

```entry caching-freshness-manifest
## 2026-08-09 · born · static-website: four rules for the data the page fetches (#727)
- **Reason:** a stale file carries a perfectly valid hash of itself, and an internal `"version"`
  field states which generation it is, never whether that generation is current, so caching the
  manifest does not save a round-trip: it moves the staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor
  is length a stand-in for a hash, since a correction applied uniformly across a file is routinely
  byte-length-neutral: the timezone fix rewriting every `16:25` to `17:25` moved 0 bytes of a 3.1 MB

  entry as it is written, so the check is a string compare rather than megabytes through a digest on
  the critical path of every load.
```

```entry caching-freshness-manifest
## 2026-08-09 · born · static-website: four rules for the data the page fetches (#727)
- **Reason:** a stale file carries a perfectly valid hash of itself, and an internal `"version"`
  field states which generation it is, never whether that generation is current, so caching the
  manifest does not save a round-trip: it moves the staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor
  is length a stand-in for a hash, since a correction applied uniformly across a file is routinely
  byte-length-neutral: the timezone fix rewriting every `16:25` to `17:25` moved 0 bytes of a 3.1 MB
  catalogue while changing the meaning of every record in it. Record the manifest's hash beside the
  entry as it is written, so the check is a string compare rather than megabytes through a digest on
  the critical path of every load.
```

{"number":1645,"title":"Legacy behaves like deprecated: the guideline, the annotation, and the advisories","body":"Closes #1637

A legacy tolerance was the one thing this corpus could add with no removal written and nothing
telling its holders to move. The audit found ~28 declaration sites across `engine/` and `packs/`;
none warned anybody, and `engine/version.mjs` carried a stated end date that had passed six days
earlier with nothing arranged to notice.

## The guideline (`packs/basics`, portable)

`RULES.md` gains one rule — a tolerance is scaffolding: it ships with an advisory firing where the
old shape is still in use, and with its removal already a link in the migration's chain, gated on a
condition that reads back true rather than on a date. The *Planning a migration* bullet names that
removal among the code written before approval, and `writing-migration-plans` gains the section
behind it: the three things that ship with a tolerance, why a date gate fails in both directions,
making an unreadable gate the chain's **first link** rather than a caveat in the removal's brief,
and the asymmetry that decides between a narrow policy and `nothing`.

## The advisories — the half that reaches the holders

| Rule | Reads | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| `legacy-shape-in-use` (lifecycle) | the repo's own declaration and stamp | retired file name, `claudinite`/`maintenance` blocks, top-level `packConfig`, `taskScheduler.endpoints`, the `local_packs/` prefix, a renamed pack id, an integer version, the `updates` alias |
| `legacy-task-fields` (tasks) | `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` **source** | `agent_preprocessing*`, `prework*`, `after`, and the one-word outcome ceilings |
| `legacy-check-spellings` (growth) | `declared-checks.json` | the pre-merge `eachValueInParsedArray` spelling |
| `cer/release-workflows` (chrome-extension) | the orchestrator | its tolerated `@main` shape, which used to return silently |

All advisory, permanently: the old shape works, so none of these may stop a member's build. Each
names the edit that moves the repo forward. The task rule reads *source* because the contract's
door renames the fields away before anything downstream can see them — which is exactly what made
that tolerance invisible. Engine constants are namespace-imported and `typeof`-guarded: the two
lanes converge on separate cycles, so a pack sits beside an engine that predates a symbol, and
there the advisory simply drops rather than faulting the pack.

## The annotation — the half that schedules the removal

Every legacy declaration now carries `// @legacy-tolerance advisory:<rule|none> retire:#<issue>`
directly above it, so `grep -rn '@legacy-tolerance' engine packs` **is** the register.
`legacy-tolerance-scheduled` (local pack, blocking after its grace) holds both halves: a tolerance
with nothing above it, and an annotation the register cannot parse. It anchors at column 0, which
is what tells a tolerance point from a `const legacy =` inside a function, and its test runs it
against the real tree rather than only a fixture.

`advisory:none` claims no member file can hold the old shape; the local pack's rule obliges the
retire issue to say what does read the holder instead.

## The removals

#1638 tracks them as four links, each an ad-hoc queue item behind #1639 (the one human step: the
fleet clearance report has to exist in Shepherd before anything here can read a gate) with a
`Not-before:` giving the fleet a month of converges. #1640 and #1641 are `Automerge: nothing` —
a member holding a retired spelling gets *no* pack, loses the `update` task that would deliver its
repair, and the only way back is a hand-run against that repo. #1642 carries a narrow
predicted-folder policy; #1643 stays `nothing` because it spans four packs by construction.

`engine/version.mjs`' tolerance is re-gated here on the fleet's own state rather than the date it
missed.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 3127 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_world` 0 blocking,
`ci-work-scope` clean. Each new check was seen failing before it was believed: the annotation check
against a stripped annotation in `settings-file-names.mjs`, and `legacy-shape-in-use`'s test with
two of its branches disabled (3 of 11 tests failed).

{"number":2046,"title":"M1: the machinery's own usage file — runs, billed minutes, spend, API calls, outcomes, parks, latencies","body":"Link **M1** of #1869. Runs beside the harness lane so the numbers exist before any rewrite.

Refs #1869
Refs #1872

## What this leaves behind

- **`packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/tasks-usage-fold/`** — `agent_model: none`, a code-work worker, delivered through `deliver-generated`, writing `.claudinite/local/tasks-usage.GENERATED.json`. The machinery's own past-data plane, independent of `usage.GENERATED.json`.
- **A `claudinite-run-cost v1 …` record printed by every scheduler tick and executor run.** The format joins the two execution records in `src/items/run-record.mjs`, the record formats' single home. The API calls are counted at `src/world/github.mjs` itself — the one place every call this pack makes passes through.
- **The dashboard's model reads the new file beside the old one**, for this repo (`view-repo.mjs`) and for every member in the fleet sweep (`view-fleet.mjs`), decoded off the header the file declares for itself, with no import from the pack that writes it. Rendering is M2.

## The two parks this link was predicted to take — one of them did not happen

**The print sites do park it, as predicted.** They sit outside the item's `Merge:` policy (line numbers on the current head, `dcb7a3d`):

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/src/schedule/run.mjs` — the stopwatch at **line 572**, the phase boundaries at **lines 580, 596, 646, 651, 655 and 784**, and the print at **line 788**.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/src/execute/loop.mjs` — the per-item stamp built at **line 652**, the stopwatch at **line 726**, the run's own print at **line 747**, and the phase boundaries inside the drain loop and at **lines 422 and 541**.

**The `.gitattributes` seed did not.** The engine's converge already writes `*GENERATED* merge=ours` into the mount's own `.gitattributes` (`engine/converge-wiring.mjs`), and that glob covers `.claudinite/local/tasks-usage.GENERATED.json` with no new line and no engine change. Nothing outside the policy was touched for it.

Three other things also fall outside the policy and are part of why this parks: the pack `README.md`'s layout row, the test files (the policy names `tasks/`, `src/world/`, `src/items/` and the dashboard, none of which is `test/`), and `test/sim/world/github.mjs` — the fake port has to gain the two names the real one did, or `parity.test.mjs` goes red. The policy is left exactly as the plan predicted it — a policy that fails is the speed bump, not an error to route around.

## Readings I took where the ask was open

- **Where an executor run's record rides.** The issue says the terminal comment. An executor run drains several items and its phases are the run's, so the record is stamped on **every** item the run settles — the terminal comment where the executor converges it, the hand-off comment where a session takes it on, that being the run's last word on that item. Each stamp is a snapshot of counters that only grow, so the fold keys them by run id and keeps the **largest**. A stamp is written *during* the convergence it belongs to, so an item's own converge time is never in its own stamp; every figure is a floor, one-directionally, and the complete reading is the one the run prints into its log.
- **Every tier is appended once.** The session fold recomputes its day rows from capture files it re-reads for free. Every source here is a watermarked REST listing, so nothing is recomputed and a counting fix applies forward only. Stated in the task README rather than implied.
- **One read per item, not two.** The four latencies need label events and the cost record needs comments, so this fold reads each closed item's **timeline** once rather than its events listing and its comments separately.
- **The week tier drops `runCosts`.** A week's keys freeze forever, so a map keyed by run id would grow the file by a row's worth a week with nothing ever pruning it; its numbers survive as the week's own scalars. `latency` is kept, unique keys and all, because the samples *are* the week-level answer a quantile is taken over.
- **The precondition.** `runs-since-fold` holds while the file's own `runsFoldedThrough` still stands before the scheduler's most recent anchor. That is the mark's own movement — false the moment a fold catches up, true again at the next tick — and it costs no API call, which matters on a term asked at every tick. No built-in movement term can see the machinery: they all read the project's commits, issues, PRs and captures, and a repo whose only activity is its own queue is silent by all four.
- **`spend` and `actionsMinuteRate`.** Unset leaves **no key anywhere**, never a zero. The rate the file was priced at is written into the file beside the numbers, so a rate changed later cannot silently re-price rows frozen under the old one.

## The API budget

Per fold: two run listings, flat; one jobs listing per unseen run; at most four job-log reads (two scheduler ticks, at most two jobs each); one issues listing page; one timeline read per item closing for the first time. `read-run-costs.test.mjs` asserts the run half is under ten calls for a representative day at this repo's cadence, and that the log-read bound binds however many ticks are waiting. `MAX_RUN_READS` is the runaway guard rather than the budget — it stops, holds the watermark at the last run measured, and says so.

## What I could not verify, and what it needs

#1872 asks for the billed-minutes rounding rule to be **verified against GitHub's billing documentation at run time and cited**. A session in this repo cannot reach `docs.github.com` at all — the egress proxy refuses the domain outright (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`), for `curl` and `WebFetch` alike — so this half of the ask is unmet and no later unattended pass here can meet it either.

`billedMinutes` in `read-run-costs.mjs` therefore encodes the rule **this repo already states for itself** in `src/execute/loop.mjs` — each job's runtime rounded up to the next whole minute, summed over the run's jobs — and says at the site that it is unverified, names the doc URL, and states that it is the only place the rule is encoded. Confirming it needs a person or an unblocked environment; if the docs differ, that one function is the whole change.

## Proof

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` on the current head — **3642 pass**. The six failures are `packs/claude-code-web-users-support/test/session-start.test.mjs`, which fail identically on a clean `main` and are already filed as #2031 (the suite reads the ambient `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED`, so it is red in every unattended session).
- `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` both silent locally; `test-and-conformance` green on `dcb7a3d`, and the branch is `clean` against `main`.
- See-it-fail: the log-read bound was mutated out and `read-run-costs.test.mjs` went red on exactly that case before the guard was restored. Two assertions I wrote optimistically went red on the first run and were corrected to what the code honestly does rather than the other way round — the converge and hand-off phases genuinely cannot be in the stamp written during them.
- Rebased onto `main` after #1347 landed; `parity.test.mjs` caught the fake GitHub port lacking the two names the real one gained, and the fake now counts its own requests the way the real port does.

## What is not here

The `queue`, `parks`, `taskCost` and `taskExec` writers in the session fold are marked `@deprecated` naming this file as their successor, and nothing else. Their removal is a later plan, as #1869's own corrections say.

This PR carries no `Closes` line by design: #1872's own converge owns its state (a native closing keyword would override the intended `needs-human-approval` park), and #1869 is a tracking issue this link must not close.

=== README ===
# claudinite-tasks — scheduled work

Everything whose subject is task work: the work-item queue, the executor, the task contract and
its signals, calendar/anchor math, run records, code-work, and the delivery lane a task's output
lands through. Declaring this pack is what gives a repo scheduled work; a repo that does not
declare it runs none, which is a supported state rather than a degraded one.

The mechanism itself — the state machine, the generator, the executor's protocol, urgency and
forcing, recovery — is the canon's own tasks-dispatch design document, and authoring a task is the
`writing-tasks` skill's subject. This file is the pack's own map.

## Layout

Every module sits in the ROLE it plays, and the graph between the roles is
one-directional. `contract/` and `items/` are what everything agrees on and name no
stage; `world/` holds the only modules that reach outside the run; the stages sit on
top of those and never import each other sideways or upwards. The `tasks-stage-barriers`
and `tasks-world-edges-live-in-world` checks are what hold the shape.

| Path | The role |
|---|---|
| `src/contract/` | what a task DECLARES and what its declaration means: the declaration's shape and defaults, the term vocabulary and the precondition seam every caller asks through, cadence and anchor arithmetic, the auto-merge policy engine, task discovery, dormancy |
| `src/items/` | the work item as DATA, over the vocabulary and grammar `public/` defines: the queue listings, the run record, the pick order over the open queue, the heartbeat |
| `src/world/` | the only outward edges, each a named port — `github.mjs` (every REST path this pack calls, as a named operation), `actions.mjs` (the runner's environment) with `hold.mjs` and the three env bags beside it, `sessions.mjs` (the routine fire that starts an agent), `git.mjs`, `processes.mjs`, `clock.mjs` |
| `src/signals/` | the collectors a precondition is handed, read through the ports and described in the contract's terms |
| `src/schedule/` | the tick: which declared tasks have a window open, and the items filed for them |
| `src/execute/` | the executor: claiming a ready item, running its code-work, handing it to an agent session |
| `src/session/` | what runs INSIDE a work-item session: converging the item, verifying its outcome, the exec record, dispatch resolution, and the automerge verdict as a command |
| `src/deliver/` | turning a run's output into a landed pull request or a regenerated file |
| `src/recover/` | repair: the janitor's rules, workflow-failure escalation, the dead-run continuation |
| `src/adopt/` | what an adopting repo receives: the workflows converged from the stubs, the per-repo cron minute |
| `queue/` | `tasks/implement-request/` — the engine's own built-in task. Its `task.md` is a redirect kept for work items minted before the move (retired 2026-10-15); the spec itself is `public/implement-request.md` |
| `stubs/` | the two workflow files an adopting repo receives |
| `public/` | **everything outside this pack may reference** — the vocabulary and grammar `src/` builds on, the import surface, and the documents a routine reads. See below |
| `tasks/` | this pack's own tasks: `task-janitor` (the queue's sweeps), `usage-fold` (it folds this mechanism's run records and outcome labels), `tasks-usage-fold` (what the machinery itself cost — runs, billed minutes, API calls, outcomes, parks, latencies) and `verify-production` (coded production validations — URL probes judged as code-work) |
| `worldRules/` | the task-declaration checks |
| `workRules/` | the armed-auto-merge gate (`automerge-policy-scope`) |
| `declared-checks.json` | `tasks-pack-read-through-its-surface` — the guard over this pack's published surface, which runs wherever the pack is declared |
| `test/` | the unit suite, mirroring `src/`, and `test/sim/` — the simulator and its scenario suite, the mechanism's executable spec |
| `docs/PRINCIPLES.md` | the mechanism as claims, each citing the test that proves it |
| `src/deliver/deliver-pr.md` | the landing procedure every PR-delivering task's worker is pointed at, beside the lane it describes |

## `public/` — everything outside this pack may reference

One folder, one promise: **a name in `public/` does not move.** Everything a routine reads, another
pack imports or a member's own local pack names lives here, and nothing else of this pack is
addressable from outside. A member's `.github/workflows/` runs the entry points under `src/`
named by the two stubs, which are this pack's own files and not an outside caller.

Another pack's code may import `packs/claudinite-tasks/public/*` and nothing else of this pack;
the `pack-independence` barrier's allow list names that directory, and no other pack gains an
equivalent surface by existing. **A member's own `.claudinite/local/packs/**` reads it the same
way**, through its mount (`.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/public/*`): the nightly
converge replaces `.claudinite/shared/` and may never touch a member's own packs, so an import
aimed anywhere else is one this repository cannot repair when the layout behind it moves.

### Documents named from outside

| Path | What names it |
|---|---|
| `instructions.md` | a repo's work-item routine, as a stored prompt in its console settings |
| `implement-request.md` | the machine block of every issue adopted into the queue |

### Modules other packs import

Three of the five are the DEFINITION, and `src/` imports them from here: the vocabulary, the
grammar over it and the GitHub client import nothing of `src/`. The other two are the
machinery's own operations under a stable name.

| Module | What it publishes |
|---|---|
| `task-constants.mjs` | every value the queue writes and reads: the work item's labels, markers and body fields, the leases, the commit trailers, the declaration defaults, the pack's own parameters, the two workflow file names |
| `work-item-grammar.mjs` | the parse and serialize over that vocabulary — the title grammar that is an item's identity, the status and outcome decode over its labels (every legacy spelling included), the body fields, the machine block, the commit trailer |
| `github.mjs` | the GitHub client (`makeGh` and the run's call count), `dispatchWorkflow`, and the tracker issue a recurring task logs every run to |
| `delivery.mjs` | `deliverGenerated` — a regenerated file landed on a pull request that lands itself — and the landing lane's five names for a worker that lands its own pull request |
| `task-declaration.mjs` | the declaration's executable contract: the loader, its validation, the precondition evaluator the executor runs at pick, and the auto-merge policy engine |

A module publishes **named** exports rather than `export *`: the list in the file is the promise,
so a reader sees the whole surface in one place and an internal rename can neither widen nor
narrow it. A consumer needing something absent asks for the named export to be added here —
never a deeper import, which `tasks-pack-read-through-its-surface` refuses. Who reads each name
is derived on demand: `node packs/claudinite-canon-curation/pack-surface.mjs packs/claudinite-tasks`
renders the surface and its consumers from the tree.

A pack whose **non-task** code reads any of the modules above declares `requires: ['claudinite-tasks']`. A
pack's `tasks/` folder needs no declaration: a mount without this pack carries no `tasks/` at all,
since a task folder is inert without the queue that runs it.

## Adoption

The two workflow files and the routine endpoints cannot converge into place — `.github/workflows/`
is the one directory a member's nightly update may never write — so they are scaffolded once, at
adoption, by the `adopt-pack` skill. They are static from then on: the per-repo cron minute and
anchor hours are written once, secrets travel as one fixed line, and the `run:` lines name mount
pack paths behind which everything converges nightly.

## Checks

| Rule | Confidence | Dimension | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-code-work-env` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `automerge-policy-scope` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `legacy-task-fields` | low | complexity | check: advisory |
| `executor-workflow-secrets` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `tasks-pack-read-through-its-surface` | high | correctness | declared check: blocking |
| `repo-variables-through-the-bag` | high | correctness | declared check: blocking |

`tasks-pack-read-through-its-surface` is this pack's, not the canon's, because the consumers that
can get it wrong are members: it scans a repo's own `packs/` **and** its `.claudinite/local/packs/`,
the tree no converge may rewrite, so a deep import written there is caught in that repo's own run
rather than when it crashes. Declared here so every repo declaring this pack runs it — a canon-only
pack would never reach them (missingbulb/Shepherd#613).

`repo-variables-through-the-bag` — a module reads a repository variable over the REST variables
API, which the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused on in every member (403, and no `permissions:` key
grants it), so the read never answers. Every repository variable already travels in the executor's
vars bag: a task's code-work finds it in `process.env`, engine code reads `varsBag(env)`. Declared
for the same reason as the check above — a member's own local task is where the next such read is
written.

The first two are relevance-first — inert until the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.json` of its own; the third is self-gating on the branch's own arming trailer.

- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal — no `preconditions` saying when it runs, an unknown condition, an illegal value — so the task never fires or fires wrong.
- `task-code-work-env` — a task reads a `CLAUDINITE_*` variable code-work never sets, so a parameter (a scope filter, a dry-run switch) silently never arrives and the run goes green in its most dangerous mode.
- `executor-workflow-secrets` — the executor workflow does not pass a secret the tasks of this repo's packs declare, so the queue picks the item up and only the run finds out the secret is not there. The list is the tasks' alone; an invocation endpoint's `tokenSecret` is config, stamped by the converge and reported by the invocation call itself. Advisory because the remedy is a human-merged PR to `.github/workflows/`, the one fix a member's own machinery cannot make.
- `automerge-policy-scope` — a branch that stamped the `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy` trailer (its run intends to land its own PR) carries a diff its declared policy does not cover, which is exactly the unreviewed change the policy exists to stop.

## 2026-09-20 · born · the method for filling a pack's empty files from its history (#2176)
- **Source:** the provenance design (#2136), section 6.
- **Reason:** the judgment is what the pass is for, which sentence of a README is history, which
  commit was the decision, which field the evidence carries; so it is a skill a session loads, one
  pack per pull request, and no task, because the work ends when the last file fills.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner) approved the design; the session that wrote #2176 landed it.
- **Model:** Claude, per the commit trailer.
- **Mechanism:** a workflow skill reached for by description, never forced: its moment is a pack
  with empty files, which no file edit predicts.
- **Retire when:** the shelf's last empty file fills; the skill then serves a pack that joins the
  shelf later, or goes.
- **Landed:** #2176.

## 2026-09-20 · reworded · a file the conversion filled is on the worklist, its entry read as evidence
- **Source:** #2180, where the backfill replaced the conversion's placeholder `born` on
  declarative-content-set-icon.md with the element's four-entry history.
- **Reason:** the owner's call that the correct history is written and the growth rule only advises;
  the converted text is evidence for the entries it becomes, never dropped.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude, per the commit trailer.

## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the run starts from a brief the tool derives, not from evidence read per element
- **Source:** step 4 of #2169, 37 packs and 692 empty files after chrome-extension; the survey
  behind the change found that a squash commit here carries the pull request's body and model
  trailer, that 82 corpus-wide sweeps dominated every element's raw history, and that 305 of the 692
  elements had one pack-local commit.
- **Reason:** the judgment the pass exists for is per decision, and a decision is a commit; reading
  evidence per element re-derives each commit once per element it touched and pays the sweeps' noise
  every time. `brief` writes the commit once with every field git vouches for and `apply` fans the
  decision out, so a session spends its attention on Reason and Rejected and a giant pack fits one
  session.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner) asked for the tooling before any further backfill; the session
  that wrote it landed it.
- **Model:** Claude Fable 5.1, per the commit trailer.
- **Rejected:** a sweep ledger shared across packs (a canon-only concern the tool need not know);
  filtering version-bump commits by their subject (the bump is detected structurally, from a diff
  that changes only a version line).
- **Retire when:** the shelf's last empty file fills and no member's local pack is left to backfill;
  the commands then serve a pack that joins later, or go with the skill.

## 2026-09-21 · reworded · `_pack.md` holds the pack's shape, and the manifest's header is trimmed like the README
- **Source:** the owner's review of #2190, on the brief drafting every manifest commit onto `_pack`.
- **Reason:** a `_pack` entry is a decision about the pack - what its `pack.mjs` header comment
  already records: why it exists, why it fingerprints so, what it carries - never every change in
  the pack's scope; so the brief drafts the pack's birth only, quotes the header as the evidence,
  and lists the manifest's later commits for the session to judge, and the run trims the header once
  its decisions are entries.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude Fable 5.1, per the commit trailer.
- **Landed:** #2190.

## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the brief carries the evidence the first backfill derived by hand (#2169)
- **Source:** the first pack run under the skill, web-scraping (#2205): four of the pack's decisions
  were invisible to the brief and cost roughly as much git archaeology to find as reading its pull
  requests cost in total.
- **Reason:** the drafts cover what a carrier's own text shows changing, which is less than the
  pack's history; the steps now work the commit inventory, the version rows and the README's
  sections, which is where the rest of it was. The run also learned three things no step carried:
  load changing-pack-elements up front, since apply writes past the pre-edit guard and nothing holds
  the run until Stop; write the entries in hyphens, since no-new-long-dashes otherwise fires once
  per file; and split a per-element Source no finer than the evidence names.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner), who asked what the first run had taught the skill.
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5.
- **Landed:** #2169

## 2026-09-21 · reworded · step 10 told the run to expect silence from a command that always prints
- **Source:** a three-model comparison running this skill on `host-page`; two of the three runs
  stopped to reconcile `check <pack>`'s file-to-carrier listing against the step's wording before
  concluding the pack was clean.
- **Reason:** `check` prints the listing on a clean pack as on a faulty one, so "reporting nothing"
  is never true and a run reading it literally treats a pass as a failure.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude

```entry deciding-long-published
## 2026-08-09 · born · static-website: four rules for the data the page fetches (#727)
- **Reason:** there is no server here to vary `Cache-Control` per file, so the freshness policy
  moves into the client, and a per-file TTL reprices the same bet on every file and gets it wrong
  in both directions at once: too long and visitors read stale data, too short and they re-download
  what never changed. A content manifest buys longer caching and fresher data together, which no
  TTL can offer, and the extra request is usually one the page already makes for a version string.
  A mismatch mid-deploy is expected, so refetch once; only a disagreement surviving fresh copies of
  both is a fault.
- **Retire when:** these sites gain a server that can set per-file headers.
```

```entry caching-freshness-manifest
## 2026-08-09 · born · static-website: four rules for the data the page fetches (#727)
- **Reason:** a stale file carries a perfectly valid hash of itself, and an internal `"version"`
  field states which generation it is, never whether that generation is current, so caching the
  manifest does not save a round-trip: it moves the staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor
  is length a stand-in for a hash, since a correction applied uniformly across a file is routinely
  byte-length-neutral: the timezone fix rewriting every `16:25` to `17:25` moved 0 bytes of a 3.1 MB
  catalogue while changing the meaning of every record in it. Record the manifest's hash beside the
  entry as it is written, so the check is a string compare rather than megabytes through a digest on
  the critical path of every load.
```

# Python

Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
`python-optional-deps` skill.

## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`

The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`), so installing the package is cheap and the
heavy stack is pulled only when a user opts into the feature that needs it.

The payoff is a test suite that runs anywhere with no ML/native toolchain: the offline
and mock paths exercise the whole pipeline, and CI never has to install TensorFlow or
Torch to be green. If a `pip install <pkg>` with no extra can't import the core, a heavy
dependency has leaked into the base set — move it to an extra. Whether a given dependency
is "heavy" enough to belong in an extra is a judgment about the package's shape, which is
why this stays prose.

## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra

Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one. That
stdlib backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on, so the
full pipeline is exercised end-to-end without the ML or native stack ever being
installed. The heavy backend is then just one more implementation of the interface,
selected at runtime, never a hard import the core or the tests depend on. The clean
shape is a tiny backend interface plus a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the
*selected* backend by name — so the module that wires backends together never imports
any of them at load time, and adding a heavy backend never taxes the core.

## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression

An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter

# Python

Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
`python-optional-deps` skill.

## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`

The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
to an extra.

## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra

Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.

## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression

An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.

Declarative task preconditions, and the repo-active silence gate (#1583)

* Declarative task preconditions, and the repo-active silence gate

A task declares `preconditions`: a list of named conditions the engine
evaluates over the collected signals, and the task runs only when every
listed condition holds. `['X', 'Y || Z']` is `X && (Y || Z)` — the comma is
deliberately the opposite of an `automerge` list's, because one field grants
and the other requires — with `||` inside a term, `none` as the empty
precondition, and inline `:` arguments.

`precondition-policy.mjs` sits beside the merge-policy engine and evaluates
at the one place a verdict has ever been formed: the executor's pick and the
scheduler's planning read. It is the merge engine's mirror image in its fail
direction — an unknown term, a malformed argument or an unreadable signal is
`{ error }`, a failed run in the queue's failure lane, never a decline. A
decline would be permanent, silent staleness that nothing in the repo goes
red over.

`precondition_signals` is derived from the expression rather than declared,
so the collector union cannot disagree with what the gate consults. The
legacy `precondition` function stays accepted forever — nothing converges a
member's own local task files — and a declaration carries exactly one of the
two, enforced by the contract and read statically by
`task-declaration-shape`, which can now report unknown terms and bad
arguments at author time. A task whose gate is its own ships a
`preconditions.mjs` beside its `task.mjs`; four do.

THE SILENCE GATE: no task runs on a silent repo unless its declaration says
so, and it says so positively — `repo-active` for the calendar-triggered
tasks whose value is zero on a repo nobody works in, and nothing at all for
the movement-gated ones, which are silence-safe by their own conditions. A
scheduled task's own output counts as silence, classified structurally: the
delivery lanes stamp `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on what they commit
and merge, and the movement conditions read that trailer, so a task added
tomorrow is classified correctly on its first run with nothing to remember
and no title regex to extend.

Scheduling is the task's own precondition; the scheduler keeps no state (#1733)

A task declares `trigger: schedule | request` — who mints an occurrence — and
`preconditions` says only what must then hold, judged identically whichever
asked. The cadence is a term over the task's own run history, so the engine
keeps no calendar and no schedule board: every tick asks every scheduled task,
a decline is a log line, and one live item per task is the only invariant.

`task:origin:manual` splits a pulled run of a declared task from somebody's own
issue adopted as the work item. `frequency` and `none` are retired behind a door,
`trigger` is derived for a declaration stating none, and the nightly update
writes both into members' own declarations.

{"number":467,"title":"Tighten every RULES.md to when + what + one non-obvious fact","body":"Closes #466

Every rule in every `RULES.md` — all 18 with rules in them, canon packs plus the local `claudinite` pack — now reads as trigger (when it applies) + instruction (what to do) + at most one clause of why, kept only where the rule would otherwise land as ceremony a reader skips. **17,127 → 15,220 words (−11%)**, structure unchanged everywhere.

## Files

| File | Words |
|---|---|
| `packs/basics` | 1070 → 846 |
| `packs/research-project` | 3299 → 3127 |
| `packs/spec-driven-product` | 1704 → 1506 |
| `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite` | 1563 → 1273 |
| `packs/executable-requirements` | 1466 → 1384 |
| `packs/chrome-extension` | 1147 → 1058 |
| `packs/aws-sam` | 984 → 885 |
| `packs/web-speech` | 991 → 966 |
| `packs/firebase` | 747 → 679 |
| `packs/flutter` | 744 → 740 |
| `packs/html` | 469 → 371 |
| `packs/leaflet` | 503 → 317 |
| `packs/python` | 496 → 362 |
| `packs/firebase-release` | 456 → 442 |
| `packs/sheepdog` | 367 → 307 |
| `packs/product-wiki` | 351 → 344 |
| `packs/node` | 201 → 145 |
| `packs/tidy-repo` | 211 → 191 |

The four stub packs (`android`, `ios`, `app-store-release`, `play-store-release`) hold a "no rules captured yet" note and no rules, so they are untouched.

## What was cut

- **Enumerations restating the verb** — `hostContains` "matches any host containing that substring"; "Support is then claimed, proven, and counted like any requirement".
- **The action restated as steps** — "don't carry one approval forward"; "Always check the fancier route against the naive one before keeping it"; "Add each custom header to the allowed-headers list".
- **Consequence prose arguing for the rule** — "a padded update is worse than none"; "an unqualified `firebase deploy` in a README eventually ships someone's half-finished hosting directory"; "Reading rules and believing them is how the merge-semantics bugs above ship".
- **Hedges and provenance** — "the assessment itself stays judgment"; "so one-member kinds are normal rather than a smell"; leaflet's five `(Grounded in js/app.js …)` notes, which restate the rule and point at one project's tree from a project-agnostic pack.
- **Incident narratives in the local pack** — outage durations, owner-turn tallies, "this bit once in #NNN". The mechanism, the instruction, and every path/command stayed; only the argument for why the rule earned its place went.

## What was preserved

No rule merged, none dropped — every file's paragraph, list, and heading structure maps one-to-one onto the original. Concrete details survive verbatim: the `Comment class:` literal the `comment-classification` check enforces, the promotion ladder, `--disable-warning`/`eslint-disable` and the at-site placement rule, the `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy id, the `runScripts: "dangerously"` fix, `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`, `VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`, the leaf-id regex, and every file path and link.

Where cutting a clause would have changed what someone does, it stayed — e.g. the suppression rule's "**not** a small fix" (its link back to the preceding warnings rule) and "so no second justification is recorded elsewhere" (it tells you not to file one).

## Testing

- `node --test "engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs" "packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs"` — 622 pass, 0 fail.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — exit 0.

## 2026-09-18 · born · converted from references.md (check:gp/deploy-workflow)
- **Reason:** The deploy runs from the repo's own `.github/` because GitHub runs a Pages deploy only
  from a workflow job in the repo's own tree, never from the mount — so the pack holds the
  template and each repo hosts a managed copy. The check holds the copy present, dispatch-only and
  current, and holds every other workflow off the Pages actions, because a second publisher or a
  push trigger deploys a tree with no version cut and no park lane, and its green run looks exactly
  like success.
- **Mechanism:** a check
- **Retire when:** Retire it if the vendored surface is ever replaced by something the member cannot
  hold a stale copy of.
## 2026-09-18 · born · converted from references.md (check:gp/site-config)
- **Reason:** The publish set is deliberately **additive**, and the check makes the cost of that
  choice survivable. The rejected alternative — "publish the repo except the tooling" —
  publishes every draft, note and key nobody thought to exclude, and publishes each *new* one
  silently the day it lands. Additive inverts the failure: a forgotten entry is a missing page, and
  the check catches a path that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory in the set and a set
  with no `index.html` before any of them reaches the default branch.
- **Mechanism:** a check
- **Retire when:** Retire it if the artifact ever stops being built from an explicit list.
## 2026-09-18 · born · converted from references.md (RULES-2)
- **Reason:** The release is a task rather than a push-triggered workflow because the queue owns the
  trigger, the gate, the version bump and the park lanes, and a workflow that deploys on push has
  none of them: it ships a tree with no version cut, and a red run in the Actions list reaches
  nobody (owner, 2026-09-17: the hosting packs should have "a daily release task that will bump the
  version and release if there was any change"). The wake command is in the rule because a session
  that wants the site deployed now would otherwise reach for a push or a dispatch of its own.
- **Mechanism:** prose
- **Retire when:** Retire the rule if the deploy ever becomes idempotent against a second publisher.
## 2026-09-18 · born · converted from references.md (RULES-1)
- **Reason:** The trap is that every local preview — `file://`, `python -m http.server`, most dev
  servers — serves the site at a domain root, so a root-relative URL is correct there and wrong
  only once deployed, where nothing reports it but a 404 on the live page. A **custom domain** moves
  the site back to the root and makes the rule moot for that repo, which is why the rule states the
  subpath as the default rather than as an absolute.
- **Mechanism:** prose
- **Retire when:** Retire it if these sites ever standardise on custom domains, or if the local
  preview is replaced by one that serves from the repo subpath.
# GitHub Pages

- **Writing a link, asset path or `fetch` in a page** — make it relative to the page, never
  root-relative: Pages serves the site at `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/`, so `/style.css`
  resolves above the site and 404s in production while working in every local preview.
  (writing-link-asset)

- **Wanting the site deployed now, or from a workflow of your own** — never add a workflow that
  publishes: the `site-release` task is the one path to production, it cuts the version and
  parks where a person must act, and a second publisher has none of that while its green run
  looks exactly like success. Force a release instead with (wanting-site-deployed)

  ```
  gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=github-pages/site-release
  ```

{"number":345,"title":"python: convert the lazy-import & install-hint rules into skill-owned check-the-work rules","body":"Reworks the new `python` pack to follow the pattern PR #350 established: keep the pack, add a skill for the activity, move every rule that has a false-positive-free file-scoped signature into check-the-work tests (deleting its prose so the failure message is the only copy), and keep as prose only the residue that genuinely has no such signature.

## What changed

**The pack keeps prose for the residue and now also mounts a skill.** `packs/python/pack.mjs` adds `skills: ['python-optional-deps']` (fingerprint `detect` unchanged); `RULES.md` is trimmed to the three judgment rules; `README.md`'s rule table shows how each rule is now enforced.

**New skill `python-optional-deps`** — a minimal SKILL.md (trigger + one pointer paragraph, no re-teaching so nothing drifts) and a `checks.mjs` owning two rules, discovered by `skills/registry.mjs` and run at every Stop and in CI. A shared `pyproject.mjs` holds the packaging knowledge both rules need (the declared-optional dist set, and the conservative dist→import-name mapping) — kept beside the rules, not in `checks/lib` (which carries engine mechanism only, per #351).

| Rule | Severity | Signature |
|---|---|---|
| `python-optional-import-top-level` | blocking | a module-top-level (column-0, so outside any def/try) `import`/`from` of a package the repo's own `[project.optional-dependencies]` declares optional |
| `python-optional-import-install-hint` | advisory | a `try/except ImportError` guard whose try-body imports a declared-optional package and whose except-body re-raises with no `pip install` hint anywhere in it |

## Which converted, and why / what stayed prose

The strong ground truth is the project's own `pyproject.toml`: `[project.optional-dependencies]` names *exactly* which packages are optional, so no "is this heavy?" judgment is needed to gate rules 2 and 3 — a top-level import (or an unhelpful guard re-raise) of a self-declared-optional package is a false-positive-free, file-scoped signal. Both checks are inert unless the repo declares optional deps (the RELEVANCE-FIRST gate — a skill check runs on every repo), scope only to those exact packages, skip test files, and self-exclude the skill's own dir.

- **Rule 2 (import lazily)** → `python-optional-import-top-level`, **blocking**. A guarded top-level import is indented (never column 0), so it is *not* flagged here — that shape is rule 3's domain, keeping the two clean.
- **Rule 3's "re-raise names the extra"** → `python-optional-import-install-hint`, **advisory** (whether a message names the *exact* extra is a wording judgment). A block is in scope only when its own try-body imports a declared-optional package, so an unrelated `except ImportError` (a fallback import, a feature probe) is never touched.
- **Stayed prose (documented residue):** *which deps belong in the dependency-free base set* (rule 1) and *the stdlib-backend architecture* (rule 4) are genuine architecture judgment with no static signature; and *the `# noqa: F401` availability-probe suppression* (rule 3's other half) can't be told from an accidental unused import without a full unused-name analysis. A dist whose import name is unrelated to its name (`Pillow`→`PIL`) is deliberately unmapped — a safe false-negative, never a false-positive.

## Tests

17 new fixture tests (scratch-repo harness), each rule proven both directions — violating fixtures find with the right severity/line; clean ones (lazy in-function imports, guarded/indented imports, the grounded install-hint re-raise, probe guards with no raise, guards around non-optional imports, marker-less repos, `pyproject` with no optional-deps, test files, the skill's own dir) stay quiet — and mutation-tested red (neutering each `run()` fails exactly the two violating-fixture tests per rule). Full suite: **434 pass**. Whole-repo sweep: clean on content (the only finding is the pre-existing branch-update merge commit, which resolves on squash-merge). The `file-placement` `skills/` acceptance from #350 already covers the engine-lib import; catalogs (`packs/README.md` row, `skills/README.md` entry) updated for `catalog-completeness`, and the pack's `skills` list satisfies `skill-ownership`.

{"number":467,"title":"Tighten every RULES.md to when + what + one non-obvious fact","body":"Closes #466

Every rule in every `RULES.md` — all 18 with rules in them, canon packs plus the local `claudinite` pack — now reads as trigger (when it applies) + instruction (what to do) + at most one clause of why, kept only where the rule would otherwise land as ceremony a reader skips. **17,127 → 15,220 words (−11%)**, structure unchanged everywhere.

## Files

| File | Words |
|---|---|
| `packs/basics` | 1070 → 846 |
| `packs/research-project` | 3299 → 3127 |
| `packs/spec-driven-product` | 1704 → 1506 |
| `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite` | 1563 → 1273 |
| `packs/executable-requirements` | 1466 → 1384 |
| `packs/chrome-extension` | 1147 → 1058 |
| `packs/aws-sam` | 984 → 885 |
| `packs/web-speech` | 991 → 966 |
| `packs/firebase` | 747 → 679 |
| `packs/flutter` | 744 → 740 |
| `packs/html` | 469 → 371 |
| `packs/leaflet` | 503 → 317 |
| `packs/python` | 496 → 362 |
| `packs/firebase-release` | 456 → 442 |
| `packs/sheepdog` | 367 → 307 |
| `packs/product-wiki` | 351 → 344 |
| `packs/node` | 201 → 145 |
| `packs/tidy-repo` | 211 → 191 |

The four stub packs (`android`, `ios`, `app-store-release`, `play-store-release`) hold a "no rules captured yet" note and no rules, so they are untouched.

## What was cut

- **Enumerations restating the verb** — `hostContains` "matches any host containing that substring"; "Support is then claimed, proven, and counted like any requirement".
- **The action restated as steps** — "don't carry one approval forward"; "Always check the fancier route against the naive one before keeping it"; "Add each custom header to the allowed-headers list".
- **Consequence prose arguing for the rule** — "a padded update is worse than none"; "an unqualified `firebase deploy` in a README eventually ships someone's half-finished hosting directory"; "Reading rules and believing them is how the merge-semantics bugs above ship".
- **Hedges and provenance** — "the assessment itself stays judgment"; "so one-member kinds are normal rather than a smell"; leaflet's five `(Grounded in js/app.js …)` notes, which restate the rule and point at one project's tree from a project-agnostic pack.
- **Incident narratives in the local pack** — outage durations, owner-turn tallies, "this bit once in #NNN". The mechanism, the instruction, and every path/command stayed; only the argument for why the rule earned its place went.

## What was preserved

No rule merged, none dropped — every file's paragraph, list, and heading structure maps one-to-one onto the original. Concrete details survive verbatim: the `Comment class:` literal the `comment-classification` check enforces, the promotion ladder, `--disable-warning`/`eslint-disable` and the at-site placement rule, the `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy id, the `runScripts: "dangerously"` fix, `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`, `VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`, the leaf-id regex, and every file path and link.

Where cutting a clause would have changed what someone does, it stayed — e.g. the suppression rule's "**not** a small fix" (its link back to the preceding warnings rule) and "so no second justification is recorded elsewhere" (it tells you not to file one).

## Testing

- `node --test "engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs" "packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs"` — 622 pass, 0 fail.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — exit 0.

content.content:
* A task cadence measures whole UTC periods, not a per-repo anchor

`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, `weeklyDay` and `monthlyDay` let a repo move the
boundaries its cadences were measured against. The design reason for that was
ordering members an hour ahead of the canon, and #1995 measured this repo's own
cron across a week: the morning fire time moved 68 minutes and the evening one
78, both wider than the 60-minute stagger the ordering rested on. What the knob
did reliably was put a seam inside every day. Before the anchor hour the current
period was still yesterday's, so one run read as consumed at 03:00 and as open at
09:00, and "has it run today" was never the question the term answered.

So a period is now the UTC calendar and nothing else: a day opens at midnight, a
week on the Sunday that opened it, a month on its 1st. `anchorInstant` takes a
cadence and an instant, `evaluatePreconditions` takes no schedule, and two repos
asked at the same moment get the same answer.

The term that states it is `schedule:at-most-<daily|weekly|monthly>`, which says
what it is out loud: a rate limit on the scheduler's own asking, never a claim
that there is work to do. `due:<cadence>` is the same function under the name it
was introduced with, accepted permanently for the reason LEGACY_FREQUENCIES is,
and rewritten at the door so one spelling reaches every reader downstream.
`last-run-over:` is deleted; no declaration in the canon used it.

The scheduler workflow's two cron hours came off the same setting. They are now
derived from the repo name beside the minute, written once when the file is
scaffolded, and preserved by every converge after: `.github/workflows/` lands
only through a pull request a person merges, so restamping the line would put
every member's scheduler behind a human gate on every change to the derivation.
No member's cron moves.

A migration record drops the three keys from each member's own declaration and
restates its local-pack task files, with the apply stage `migration-apply-stage`
asks for: the codemod cannot see the member's own tests, and the last record to
rewrite these files landed red on a repo with five of them. The keys stay
accepted and unread until #2178, because an unknown key is a blocking settings
error and every member carries them until its own converge runs.

Closes #1995

# The GitHub Pages release

A release is one thing: the default branch's tree, deployed to Pages by the vendored
[deploy workflow](../../stubs/workflows/github-pages-deploy.yml), which the
`github-pages/site-release` task dispatches at the exact commit it released — after
advancing the version, when the public-website pack is declared. The task's
[README](../../tasks/site-release/README.md) says what the worker does; this says how to
wire it, operate it, and what a change to it must not break.

=== task.json
{
  "$schema": "../../../claudinite-tasks/task.schema.json",
  "id": "site-release",
  "description": "Deploys the default branch to GitHub Pages, advancing the site version first where public-website is declared so the repo records what went out. The upload is the vendored deploy workflow, dispatched at the exact commit: the one part of a Pages release only a workflow job can run.",
  "trigger": "schedule",
  "preconditions": [
    "schedule:at-most-daily",
    "unreleased-commits"
  ],
  "expected_outcome": "no_code_changes",
  "on_interrupt": "needs-human",
  "code_work": "node worker.mjs",
  "code_work_timeout": 1800,
  "agent_model": "none"
}

# github-pages — why its rules exist

Maintenance and review only: the reason behind each rule, written so a later pass can reaffirm or
retire it. No session loads this file and no rule points a reader here.

- **(RULES-1)** The trap is that every local preview — `file://`, `python -m http.server`, most
  dev servers — serves the site at a domain root, so a root-relative URL is correct there and
  wrong only once deployed, where nothing reports it but a 404 on the live page. A **custom
  domain** moves the site back to the root and makes the rule moot for that repo, which is why
  the rule states the subpath as the default rather than as an absolute. Retire it if these sites
  ever standardise on custom domains, or if the local preview is replaced by one that serves from
  the repo subpath.

- **(RULES-2)** The release is a task rather than a push-triggered workflow because the queue
  owns the trigger, the gate, the version bump and the park lanes, and a workflow that deploys on
  push has none of them: it ships a tree with no version cut, and a red run in the Actions list
  reaches nobody (owner, 2026-09-17: the hosting packs should have "a daily release task that will
  bump the version and release if there was any change"). The wake command is in the rule because
  a session that wants the site deployed now would otherwise reach for a push or a dispatch of
  its own. Retire the rule if the deploy ever becomes idempotent against a second publisher.

- **(check:gp/site-config)** The publish set is deliberately **additive**, and the check makes
  the cost of that choice survivable. The rejected alternative — "publish the repo except the
  tooling" — publishes every draft, note and key nobody thought to exclude, and publishes each
  *new* one silently the day it lands. Additive inverts the failure: a forgotten entry is a
  missing page, and the check catches a path that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory
  in the set and a set with no `index.html` before any of them reaches the default branch.
  Retire it if the artifact ever stops being built from an explicit list.

- **(check:gp/deploy-workflow)** The deploy runs from the repo's own `.github/` because GitHub
  runs a Pages deploy only from a workflow job in the repo's own tree, never from the mount — so
  the pack holds the template and each repo hosts a managed copy. The check holds the copy
  present, dispatch-only and current, and holds every other workflow off the Pages actions,
  because a second publisher or a push trigger deploys a tree with no version cut and no park
  lane, and its green run looks exactly like success. Retire it if the vendored surface is ever
  replaced by something the member cannot hold a stale copy of.

{"number":1634,"title":"Every pack's RULES.md carries rules, not a description of the pack","body":"Closes #1632

The same audit #1625 got, across the other 25 packs. Every one opened its `RULES.md` with a paragraph describing what the pack covers ("Portable, project-agnostic practices for …", "This document defines how the owner wants … run"), and several framed their sections the same way. It changes nothing a session does, every session in every declaring repo pays for it, and each pack's `README.md` plus its manifest's `ruleRoutingGuidance` (what renders into `directory.GENERATED.md`) already carries it — I checked each one before dropping it.

**Dropped:** 25 intro paragraphs; the playbook framing in `research-project` and `spec-driven-product` (what the class is, "a default to adapt, not a contract"); `basics`'s four section preambles, including the skill list the session's own skill roster already carries; `headless-browser`'s scope note; `macos`'s "these are the rules that cost the most to learn" and "Two consequences"; `node`'s "Two that recur".

**Kept as rules, re-keyed:** `macos`'s usage-description paragraph becomes **Reaching for a protected resource**; `research-project`'s interaction-cadence paragraph becomes two bullets; `python`'s three section-shaped rules become trigger-keyed bullets at the ration (280 → 150 words).

**Left alone:** the paragraph-form instruction in `executable-requirements` and `research-project` — it is prose-shaped, but it instructs, and rewriting it is a rewrite of substance rather than this sweep. Corpus non-rule prose is 2,900 → 1,080 words, and what remains is nearly all of that kind. Those two, plus `spec-driven-product`, read as manuals whose procedure would sit better in a skill; worth a separate look.

Pack READMEs take the two new rule rows (`macos`, `research-project`) and recounted word columns where a dropped preamble had been counted into a rule. Every touched pack bumps its version with a `VERSIONS.md` row.

Suite 3104/3104, `check_the_work` clean, `check_the_world` 0 blocking.

| Pack | Skill | Forced for |
|---|---|---|
| basics | `writing-repo-scanning-checks` | `**/engine/checks/**`, `**/packs/*/worldRules/**`, `**/packs/*/workRules/**`, `**/packs/*/skills/*/checks.mjs`, `**/declared-checks.json` |

| firebase | `firestore-security-rules`, `firebase-functions`; `create-release-plan` gains `.firebaserc`, `firebase.json` | `**/firestore.rules`, `**/storage.rules`; `functions/**` |
| aws-sam | `sam-template`, `sam-build-and-deps` | `**/template.yaml`, `**/template.yml`; `package.json` + template |
| flutter | `flutter-golden-tests`, `flutter-pubspec` | `**/*_test.dart`, `**/test/**/*.dart`; `**/pubspec.yaml`, `**/pubspec.lock` |

| chrome-extension | `extension-host-permissions` | `**/manifest.json` |
| claudinite-fleet-sheepdog | `configuring-the-fleet` | `.claudinite-settings.json` |
| node | `node-test-discovery` | `.github/workflows/**`, `package.json`, `*/package.json` |
